http-server.title: HTTP Server (Chef Metaphor)
http-server.buddyStartMsg: Hi! I'm Bubu, your study buddy. Let's build a Node.js web server together! Load the 'http' module to start.

steps.title: Step 1: Gathering the Ingredients
steps.narrative: Imagine Node.js is a chef inside a high-speed toy factory. To build a web server, the chef needs to fetch the recipe module. In Node.js, we load core modules using the keyword require(). Let's load the 'http' module and save it in a variable called http.
steps.goalText: Write the code to load the http module:

hints.message: Make sure you use the 'require' keyword to import modules!
Double check the spelling. You need to require the module named 'http' inside quotes.
Make sure you create the variable using 'const' so it doesn't accidentally get reassigned.

steps.defaultHint: Check the syntax! It should be exactly: const http = require('http');
steps.successMsg: Success! You required the HTTP module and saved it to the http variable. Chef is ready! Module 2 unlocked. 🚀

steps.title: Step 2: Building the Server
steps.narrative: Perfect! Our chef now has the HTTP module. Next, we tell the HTTP module to prepare a server. We do this using the function http.createServer(). Let's create a server and store it inside a box called server.
steps.goalText: Type the code to create the server:

hints.message: Use the 'createServer' method from your loaded 'http' module!
Store the result in a const variable called 'server'.

steps.defaultHint: Check spelling! Syntax should look like: const server = http.createServer();
steps.successMsg: Woohoo! You created the server! Chef is standing in the kitchen ready to bake web pages. Section 3 is open!

steps.title: Step 3: Giving it an Ear (Listening)
steps.narrative: Almost there! The server is built, but it is currently sitting in absolute silence. It needs an 'ear' to listen for incoming requests from the internet. We do this by calling the server.listen() function, and telling it to monitor a numerical port like 3000.
steps.goalText: Type the code to make your server listen on port 3000:

hints.message: Call the 'listen()' method on your 'server' object.
Make sure to pass the number 3000 inside the parenthesis to listen on port 3000.

steps.defaultHint: Almost there! Syntax should be exactly: server.listen(3000);
steps.successMsg: UNBELIEVABLE! You did it! Your server is listening on port 3000. You are officially a backend engineer! 🎉

fs-read.title: Reading Files (Recipe Book)
fs-read.buddyStartMsg: Hi! Let's help Bubu and Dudu read a recipe file synchronously. Load the 'fs' module to get started!

steps.title: Step 1: Fetching the Recipe Book
steps.narrative: Now our Bubu and Dudu want to read recipes from a local recipe book file. In Node.js, files are read using the built-in File System module named 'fs'. Let's load the 'fs' module using require() and store it in a variable called fs.
steps.goalText: Write the code to load the fs module:

hints.message: Use the 'require()' keyword to import modules.
Make sure you load the module named 'fs' in quotes.
Store the loaded module in a const variable called 'fs'.

steps.defaultHint: Check syntax! It should be exactly: const fs = require('fs');
steps.successMsg: Awesome! The recipe book module 'fs' is loaded. Let's fetch a recipe sheet next! 📚

steps.title: Step 2: Scanning the Recipe Sheet
steps.narrative: Excellent! Now let's tell Bubu & Dudu to read a recipe file named 'info.txt' synchronously, decoding it as 'utf8' text. We use the function fs.readFileSync('info.txt', 'utf8') and store it in a variable called data.
steps.goalText: Read info.txt synchronously and store it in 'data':

hints.message: Use the synchronous reading function 'fs.readFileSync()'.
Pass the filename 'info.txt' as the first parameter.
Remember to specify the character encoding 'utf8' as the second parameter so it reads as plain text!
Store the output in a const variable named 'data'.

steps.defaultHint: Double check syntax! It should look like: const data = fs.readFileSync('info.txt', 'utf8');
steps.successMsg: Fantastic! The file has been successfully read and loaded into the 'data' variable. Let's look at the recipe!

steps.title: Step 3: Reading the Content Aloud
steps.narrative: You've read the file successfully! Now let's print the loaded recipe stored in the data variable to the terminal console so Bubu and Dudu can see it. We do this using console.log(data);.
steps.goalText: Log the content stored in data:

hints.message: Use 'console.log()' to print output.
Pass the 'data' variable inside the console.log parentheses.

steps.defaultHint: Check syntax! It should be exactly: console.log(data);
steps.successMsg: Delicious! You successfully read the file and logged it to the screen. Bubu and Dudu can now cook the meal! 🍽️

custom-modules.title: Custom Modules (Sous Chef)
custom-modules.buddyStartMsg: Hi! Let's help Bubu and Dudu create and export a math module. Attach the add function first!

steps.title: Step 1: Mixing the Math Helper
steps.narrative: Bubu and Dudu are acting as chef and sous chef. The sous chef wants to share a custom math recipe with the main chef. In Node.js, we export custom helper functions by attaching them to the global exports object. Let's export an add arrow function: exports.add = (a, b) => a + b;.
steps.goalText: Export the add function on exports:

hints.message: Attach the function to the exports object as 'exports.add'.
Write it as an arrow function: (a, b) => a + b

steps.defaultHint: Check syntax! It should look exactly like: exports.add = (a, b) => a + b;
steps.successMsg: Splendid! The math module now exports the 'add' function. Let's load this module in our main app script next!

steps.title: Step 2: Passing the Math Helper
steps.narrative: Great! Now let's tell Bubu to load our local custom math module './math'. For local files, we pass the relative path (starting with './') into the require() function. Let's load the module and store it inside a variable called math.
steps.goalText: Load local math module and store in math:

hints.message: Use the 'require' keyword to load modules.
Make sure to write the local path './math' in quotes inside the require parentheses.
Store the imported module in a const variable called 'math'.

steps.defaultHint: Double check spelling! Syntax should look like: const math = require('./math');
steps.successMsg: Superb! The custom math module is successfully loaded. Now let's use it to calculate some recipe ratios!

steps.title: Step 3: Serving the Combined Result
steps.narrative: We have the math module loaded. Now, let's call the exported math.add() helper to add 5 and 10, printing the result to the console. We do this inside a console.log() statement.

hints.message: Wrap the entire calculation in 'console.log()'.
Call the 'add()' method on your 'math' object.
Pass the numbers 5 and 10 as parameters.
Pass the numbers 5 and 10 as parameters.

steps.defaultHint: Check spelling and matching parentheses! Syntax should be exactly: console.log(math.add(5, 10));
steps.successMsg: Fantastic! You exported a helper function, imported it locally, and called it successfully! You've mastered Custom Modules! 🌟
